# tests/test_four.py
def test_cuts() -> None:
    assert summarize("text", FakeClient(), max_words=3) == "one two three"

# FakeClient replies: one two three four five six
why: The reply is cut to 3 words, which is what the test expects.
pytest shows the line that broke and the values it compared.

q: The assert is correct. What does pytest show?
why: pytest only runs functions whose name starts with test_. Silence is not success.
The file name must start with test_ (or end with _test.py). This one does neither.

q: The test expects the wrong value. What does pytest compare?
o: 'ok' (what the code returned) and 'ok ok' (what the test expected)
why: Read the assert line first: the left side is what your code gave, the right side is what you expected.

q: Why do we hand the client into summarize() instead of creating it inside?
o: So a test can hand in a fake: no network, no key, the same answer every time
Because it makes the code faster
why: A fake makes the test fast, free and repeatable. Real model calls are checked later with evaluation.
